idiom_name: chan Order, typed and directionally constrained (chan<- Order / <-chan Order)
implementation_notes: Go's channels are datatype channels by construction: chan Order carries nothing but Order, the compiler enforces it, and the receiver's loop therefore needs no type switch or interface assertion - the element type is the contract. Declare the direction in every signature (chan<- Order on the producer side, <-chan Order on the consumer side) so 'which side may send on this channel' is part of the API rather than a convention, and the type shown in the signature documents what the stage consumes. Across processes the same rule is one broker topic or queue per message type with a per-topic decoder; multiplexing several types onto one topic and type-switching on the payload is the interface{}-shaped version of the anti-pattern this pattern removes.
pitfalls: Assigning a directional channel to a variable of the bidirectional type loses the constraint, so the receiver can suddenly send; keep chan<- / <-chan in signatures and struct fields.

Unbuffered channels make every send a rendezvous, so one slow consumer stalls its producer; size each type's channel deliberately (or add a select with a drop/timeout policy) instead of defaulting to make(chan T).
Only producers close a channel: a consumer that closes, or two producers that both close, panic; for multiple producers use a context or quit channel and let the last writer close.
